description:
We're building PyroWatch, a wildfire intelligence dashboard focused on making satellite fire data easier to explore and understand. I’m interested in climate technology, geospatial data, and using software to support environmental monitoring. The project uses Python, Streamlit, interactive maps, data visualizations, and an experimental hotspot-prediction model.

We’d love to connect with teammates interested in contributing to a practical, socially useful project.
summary: PyroWatch is a Streamlit dashboard for monitoring NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS fire detections in Ghana. It provides interactive maps, historical trends, regional insights, rule-based alerts, and experimental next-day hotspot forecasts. It helps users identify potential fire activity for monitoring and planning but does not provide official fire warnings.
details:
What it does and how it works

PyroWatch is a wildfire-monitoring dashboard focused on Ghana and nearby areas. It brings NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS satellite thermal-anomaly observations into one interface. Users can explore detections on an interactive map, filter by date, region, sensor, and other attributes, review trends and rule-based alerts, and export filtered observations. Data can be uploaded as FIRMS CSV files or fetched through the FIRMS API. An experimental model estimates next-day hotspot likelihood from historical detection patterns and seasonality.

Benefits and intended impact

The dashboard makes large, technical satellite datasets easier to inspect and helps users notice patterns that may deserve further investigation. Its intended impact is to support situational awareness and planning by making observations and analytical signals more accessible. It is a decision-support tool, not an emergency-warning system: satellite detections are not confirmed fires, and model estimates require interpretation and verification.

Tools and development

The project uses Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Folium, and Plotly. It was developed for a Windows environment and can be deployed as a web app. FIRMS data is the primary observation source; a saved model artifact supports forecasts without requiring training CSVs at runtime.

What makes it creative

PyroWatch combines interactive mapping, clustered detections, density visualization, historical analytics, alert summaries, and regional forecasts in a single dashboard. It also keeps display data separate from model-training data, supporting a lighter deployment while preserving a local retraining workflow.

Factors considered and future plans

The project accounts for differences between MODIS and VIIRS, duplicate observations, missing detections, uncertainty in grouping nearby detections, and the limitations of satellite overpass data. Current forecasts use historical detections and seasonality; in the future, we plan to incorporate weather data to improve hotspot predictions. Any improvement will need to be evaluated carefully, and forecasts should remain clearly identified as estimates rather than official warnings.

Github Link: https://github.com/Affah-immaculate-cpu/PyroWatch
